core.text: 2 Related Works

To post-train non-reasoning base models into reasoning models, a common practice is to apply long chain-of-thought supervised fine-tuning as a cold start, followed by Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) (Guo et al., 2025; Team, 2025; Wang et al., 2025). However, since many real-world reasoning tasks are not verifiable, recent work has examined the extent to which capabilities learned via RLVR generalize beyond the training domain. Huan et al. show that RLVR on mathematical reasoning yields stronger cross-domain generalization than supervised fine-tuning, while Cheng et al. find that such generalization is uneven and that rarer tasks require additional training data to achieve performance improvements. In contrast, our work takes an orthogonal perspective by studying how RLVR affects generalization of reasoning monitorability and its relationship to reasoning capability.

Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in large reasoning models provides a potential interface for safety oversight by exposing intermediate decision-making steps (Korbak et al., 2025). Empirical studies show that CoT-based monitoring can outperform output-only monitoring in detecting hidden misalignment or unsafe intent (Arnav et al., 2025; Baker et al., 2025). However, a growing body of work identifies a key limitation: CoT traces are often not faithful to the internal computation that determines model behavior (Jacovi & Goldberg, 2020; Lanham et al., 2023; Turpin et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025a; Guan et al., 2025; Chua & Evans, 2025; Xiong et al., 2025). In particular, directly optimizing against external monitors during RLVR as a reward can degrade monitorability through reward hacking or adversarial adaptation (Baker et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a; Guan et al., 2025; MacDermott et al., 2025).

Recent work, therefore, focuses on identifying when and why CoT becomes monitorable. Emmons et al. shows that tasks requiring genuine multi-step computation increase monitorability, while Guan et al. identifies reasoning length as an important axis. MacDermott et al. further study how RL training variants, including length penalties and KL regularization, affect reasoning behavior in controlled settings. In contrast to these works, we study the monitorability property over the course of vanilla RLVR training on practical data distributions and examine its generalization and internal mechanisms.
3 Setup

This section details our experimental framework. We describe the model architectures, the diverse curation of training datasets, our RLVR training protocol, and the suite of metrics used for evaluation.
3.1 Training Details

We curate a multi-domain training corpus to systematically probe the impact of data distribution on monitorability. Our training data spans four distinct categories: Math, Code, Science, and Instruction Following (IF). Details of the training data are provided in Appendix A.1.

To study monitorability changes throughout the RLVR process, we use Qwen3-4B (Team, 2025) and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (DS-1.5B) (Guo et al., 2025) as different base models. These models have already performed long CoT cold starts.

To isolate the contribution of each data domain, we train a suite of model variants. We perform RL training using GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) for each category (Math-only, Code-only, Science-only, IF-only), where each setting restricts training to a single data distribution. Additionally, we explore multi-domain dynamics through a combined All strategy (training on the union of all datasets) and an All without IF (w/o IF) ablation to specifically measure the marginal contribution of instruction-following data. We trained all these models with 800 steps. Then, we implement an IF Cascade (IF+) strategy (Wang et al., 2025), initializing with 600 steps of general training (All without IF) followed by 600 steps of targeted IF fine-tuning. We also construct two model training ablations that use different generation lengths and two data variants that explicitly capture training-data hardness from low to high, using 400 training steps on the math dataset. Training details are provided in Appendix A.2.

We use Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct as our primary monitor, with Qwen3-30B-A3B providing alternative correlations in Appendix C.1 (Table 6). Crucially, ”monitorability” refers to the intrinsic properties of the evaluated model, independent of the monitor’s specific capabilities.

We list the checklist of our assessment in Table 1. We adopt a rigorous definition of monitorability quantified primarily by the g-mean2\text{g-mean}^{2} metric (Guan et al., 2025). g-mean2\text{g-mean}^{2} is calculated as the simple product of the monitor’s sensitivity and specificity (TPR ×\times TNR) over the CoT, with a higher score indicating better monitorability with respect to the applied monitor. To ensure our evaluation focuses on meaningful signals, we only include cases where the interventions successfully alter the model’s output in at least 5% of instances, defined in Appendix B.2.

Under this metric, we primarily use Hint-based Interventions (Chen et al., 2025a; Guan et al., 2025; Chua & Evans, 2025), and construct a broad set of evaluation tasks across Math (AMC12, Math500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021), AIME 24/25), Code (CodeMMLU (Manh et al., 2024)), Science (GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al., 2024), MMLU Science (College Biology/Physics/Chemistry) (Hendrycks et al., 2021)), and General tasks (ZebraLogic (Small/Medium/Large) (Lin et al., 2025), MedQA (Jin et al., 2021), and MMLU Global Facts (Hendrycks et al., 2020)), and each consist three hint types, as described in Appendix B.3. When reporting categorical g-mean2\text{g-mean}^{2} (e.g., Math), we typically average over the aforementioned tasks; for overall g-mean2\text{g-mean}^{2}, we average across categories.

We also follow (Guan et al., 2025) to construct Sycophancy test using Scruples test set (Lourie et al., 2021), and detect capability concealment through a Sandbagging test on WMDP subsets (bio, cyber, chem) (Li et al., 2024), details can be found in Appendix B.4 and B.5.

Beyond g-mean2\text{g-mean}^{2}, we additionally compute Draft-to-Answer (D2A) Faithfulness metrics (Draft Reliance and Draft–Answer Consistency) (Xiong et al., 2025) on a subset of tasks (AMC12, CodeMMLU, GPQA-Diamond, MedQA, MMLU Global Facts). While g-mean2\text{g-mean}^{2} measures sensitivity to external interventions, D2A assesses the causal dependence of the answer on the generated draft. This serves as a proxy to validate that g-mean2\text{g-mean}^{2} reflects genuine monitorability from reasoning traces rather than surface-level sensitivity. Details can be found in Appendix B.8.

We also list the checklist of our capability assessment in Table 1. We simultaneously track task performance to correlate monitorability shifts with capability gains. Our evaluation suite includes: Math (AMC12, Math500, and AIME 24/25), Code (CodeMMLU, HumanEval+ (Liu et al., 2023), MBPP+ (Liu et al., 2023)), Science (GPQA-Diamond, MMLU Science (College Biology/Physics/Chemistry)), General (MedQA, MMLU Global Facts, ZebraLogic), and Instruction Following (IFBench (Pyatkin et al., 2025) and IFEval (Zhou et al., 2023)).
4 The Dynamics of Monitorability Across Domains

This section presents our empirical findings on the generalization of monitorability across distributions (Section 4.1) and its relationship with model capability (Section 4.2). We study whether monitorability emerges universally during RLVR11 1 rewards are task accuracy and format only, see appendix A.2, how it evolves across different training phases, and whether it is merely a byproduct of increasing reasoning intelligence.
4.1 How Training Distribution Shapes Monitorability

Contrary to the expectation that RLVR universally improves monitorability, we find that the effect is highly distribution-dependent. Training on a specific domain does not guarantee improved monitorability within that same domain, nor does it consistently transfer to others. For example, as shown in Figure 1, training on the Science domain on Qwen3-4B even results in a slight degradation on the in-distribution science domain, and significant degradation of monitorability on Code and Sandbagging test sets. In most evaluations, we observe a characteristic pattern across domains and different intervention types: an immediate, rapid gain in monitorability followed by stagnation or a slight decline, rather than sustained improvement, consistent with the previously observed “free gift” phenomenon (Guan et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a). Interestingly, training that leverages Instruction Following (IF) data (both pure IF and the IF-mixed “ALL” dataset) often yields peak monitorability.

As shown in Figure 2, we investigate whether monitorability is transfers across domains. By correlating g-mean2\text{g-mean}^{2} scores across different evaluation task domains for the same model checkpoints, we observe a strong positive correlation between monitorability on Science, Code, and General domains. This suggests the possibility of a shared underlying factor driving monitorability. However, the Math domain emerges as a slight outlier with lower correlations, likely due to the distinct nature of free-form generation in math tasks (AIME 24/25, Math500) and the use of interventions that differ from those in other domains. This suggests potential misalignment of monitorability across task types and hints, highlighting the need for comprehensive analysis when interpreting monitorability.

To understand the temporal dynamics of monitorability development, we partition the training trajectory into two phases: early training (steps 0-300) and late training (steps 300-800). Table 2 reveals an asymmetry: the early phase consistently yields substantially larger monitorability gains than the late phase across both models and all training configurations. Specifically, the Math and Science domains alone exhibit particularly pronounced early-phase dominance, with late-phase gains often dropping to near-zero or even negative values (e.g., Qwen3-4B math shows -0.05 late-phase loss).

Among all settings, distributions containing IF data (IF, ALL) consistently achieve the highest early-phase and overall gains. This suggests that the constraint-satisfaction nature of IF tasks provides particularly strong learning signals for developing monitorable reasoning patterns during the initial stages of RLVR training. In contrast, late-phase training generally shows diminishing returns. However, the ALL distribution, which is composed of more data and spans more domains, maintains relatively stronger gains than single-domain configurations. This suggests that diverse, multi-domain exposure becomes more valuable as training progresses and early-phase gains saturate.

Given the strong monitorability gains from IF training, we ask whether IF data can also improve monitorability when introduced after a model has already been trained on other domains. This question is practically important: training on a large, mixed distribution—especially one that includes domains with expensive verification (for example, code)—can lead to substantial resource waste (Wang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b), and multi-stage RL training is itself a common practice for state-of-the-art models (Guo et al., 2025; Team, 2025).

Inspired by cascaded training regimes (Wang et al., 2025), we propose a “IF Cascade (+IF)” strategy: models are first trained for 600 steps on a mixed “All without IF” dataset, then fine-tuned for an additional 600 steps exclusively on IF data. As shown in Table 3, this +IF configuration substantially boosts monitorability relative to the w/o IF checkpoint, and this approach even surpassing both pure IF training and the fully mixed “ALL” setting. This suggests that IF data can serve as a potent “monitorability booster” even when applied after task-specific RLVR training, potentially leveraging prior task exposure while reshaping reasoning behavior toward stronger constraint satisfaction.
4.2 Is Monitorability Gain a Byproduct of Capability?

A critical question is whether monitorability is merely a byproduct of general reasoning capability. If “smarter” models are inherently more articulate and informative to its internal reasoning, we would expect a strong positive correlation between task performance and monitorability. The top row of Figure 3 confirms that task capability consistently improves throughout training in most configurations, except for IF-only training 22 2 this aligns with the observations in Pyatkin et al.. However, the correlation analysis in the bottom row of Figure 3 reveals a weak and variable relationship between capability and monitorability. For instance, for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, Math monitorability correlates positively with capability, while other domains often yield negative correlations. For Qwen3-4B, we observe negative correlations even in the Math domain, whereas Code shows a stronger positive link between capability and monitorability. This inconsistency across architectures and tasks suggests that monitorability can be orthogonal to raw reasoning capability; moreover, the highly monitorable IF-trained model shows substantial performance degradation on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, further confirming that optimizing for performance does not automatically guarantee monitorability.

We further distinguish between having Instruction Following (IF) capability and being trained on IF data. As shown in the Figure 4, for models not explicitly trained on IF data (Left plots), IF performance is weakly or even negatively correlated with monitorability. This underscores that merely possessing higher IF capability does not automatically translate to better monitorability. Even for Qwen3-4B trained with IF data (right plots), we do not observe a strong correlation. This suggests that improvements in monitorability are not a simple byproduct of increased capability. Instead, the specific nature of IF training—likely its requirement for strict constraint satisfaction—plays a causal role in aligning reasoning with output. Thus, training on IF data, rather than IF capability itself, is the primary driver of these gains.
5 Mechanistic Drivers of Monitorability Gain

To better understand monitorability, we track internal activations and aim to identify the key internal factors that drive it across training distributions and checkpoints. Specifically, we analyze the well-known distribution sharpening effect in RLVR-trained models and shifts in attention mass across segments during RLVR training.
5.1 Entropy Reduction as a Driver of Monitorability

We first investigate the relationship between the entropy of the model’s generation and its monitorability. The intuition is that RLVR training typically sharpens the policy distribution (reducing entropy) to focus on correct solution paths (Zhao et al., 2025; Yue et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Karan & Du, 2025). We question whether this sharpening process naturally contributes to the observed monitorability gains—i.e., whether a narrower, more confident output distribution implicitly shapes the reasoning behaviors more informative and monitorable. Metric definition and calculation can be found in Appendix B.6.

As shown in Figure 5 for GPQA, AMC12, CodeMMLU, and MedQA, and Figure 8 for MMLU subsets in Appendix C, the correlation between task entropy (averaged across all vanilla responses) and monitorability (g-mean2\text{g-mean}^{2}) presents a negative correlation in most cases. Specifically, for certain domains such as MedQA and GPQA, we observe a clear negative correlation (e.g., r≈−0.82r\approx-0.82 for MedQA on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B). In these cases, checkpoints with lower entropy consistently exhibit higher monitorability. This suggests that for specific complex reasoning tasks, the “free gift” of monitorability may be partially driven by the model collapsing onto a narrower set of valid reasoning patterns that are easier to monitor, rather than purely learning a new mechanism for transparency.
5.2 What Does High Monitorability Attend To?

To further dissect the internal mechanisms, we analyze how information flows over the reasoning procedures through the attention dynamics between different functional segments of the generation process (Zhang et al., 2025). We partition the model’s context into three segments: Prompt, Reasoning (the chain-of-thought trace), and Answer (the final answering after thinking draft). We then measure the aggregated attention mass flowing between these segments (e.g., A→\toR denotes the attention the answer tokens pay to the reasoning trace). Specifically, for each attention head in every layer, we compute the average attention weight allocated by tokens in the source segment to tokens in the target segment. Note that we deliberately filter out the first “<bos>” token and chat-template tokens (including thinking tokens) to ensure that the analysis is not affected by attention sinks (Xiao et al., 2023) or template bias. These values are averaged across all heads and layers to produce a single scalar representing the connectivity strength between segments (see Appendix B.7 for a formal definition).

As summarized in Figure 5 with detailed statistics in Figure 9 and Figure 10 in Appendix C.3, we correlate the changes in these cross-segment attention masses (by averaging over all vanilla task prompts) with the gains in monitorability across training. First, we find that improvements in monitorability are generally accompanied by increased cross-segment attention connectivity, supporting the intuition that transparent reasoning requires tighter integration between the problem statement, the reasoning process, and the final solution.

Second, and most surprisingly, a breakdown of the attention flows reveals that the monitorability gain is not driven by increased attention from the Answer to the Reasoning trace (A→\toR). On the contrary, we find that A→\toR attention is remarkably negatively correlated with monitorability (Figure 5). Instead, the strongest positive predictors of monitorability are the attention flows directed towards the Prompt—specifically, A→\toP and R→\toP.

Again, we acknowledge that changes in attention focus do not necessarily imply that true integration occurs within the model. However, these patterns suggest that highly monitorable models (as measured by g-mean2\text{g-mean}^{2}) may heavily ground both their reasoning and their final answers in the initial problem description (Prompt). Since the current design of monitorability evaluations (Guan et al., 2025) mostly relies on input interventions, metric sensitivity to prompt-dependence is expected. However, this creates a potential risk of a “false sense of monitorability”: a model might achieve a high g-mean2\text{g-mean}^{2} score simply by overfitting to the prompt’s constraints, without necessarily establishing a strong causal link between its reasoning and its answer. If the answer depends more on the prompt than on the reasoning trace, the reasoning could be a faithful-looking rationalization rather than the true cause of the decision. This motivates our subsequent investigation into non input intervention based metrics to verify if the reasoning-to-answer link is genuinely robust.
6 Validating Monitorability with Draft-to-Answer Faithfulness

To complement our input-intervention-based g-mean2\text{g-mean}^{2} metric, we introduce Draft-to-Answer (D2A) Faithfulness (Xiong et al., 2025), a metric that evaluates whether the model’s final decision is causally determined by its reasoning draft. Unlike g-mean2\text{g-mean}^{2} which perturbs the input, D2A operates by intervening on the end of the generated thinking draft (e.g., swapping the conclusion) and measuring if the final answer updates accordingly. We directly use the generated GPQA and MMLU Global Facts datasets provided by Xiong et al., and we follow their pipeline to construct evaluation datasets for CodeMMLU, AMC12, and MedQA by generating initial reasoning drafts with a stronger model (Qwen3-32B) to ensure draft quality (formal definitions and construction details are in Appendix B.8).

We provide the detailed results of this metric across datasets and in Figure 11, Appendix C.4, and analyze the correlation between our primary g-mean2\text{g-mean}^{2} metric and this D2A alternative in Figure 6. For Qwen3-4B, we observe a strong positive correlation between the two metrics across most tasks. This suggests that models which show high monitorability through input intervention (high g-mean2\text{g-mean}^{2}) are also likely to be faithfully conditioned on their reasoning drafts (high D2A). For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, while reasoning-heavy tasks like Math (AMC12) align well, the correlation varies more significantly in general domains. Crucially, given this strong correlation in most reasoning tasks, the intervention-based monitorability evaluation (g-mean2\text{g-mean}^{2}) appears to be an effective proxy for internal faithfulness, even though D2A manipulates the end of the draft while g-mean2\text{g-mean}^{2} manipulates the prompt. This convergence of evidence from two distinct intervention points strengthens our confidence in the measured monitorability trends. However, the divergence in specific domains (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on general tasks), together with the strong correlation between cross-segment attention shifts toward the prompt and monitorability gains, suggests that further investigation into metric robustness is warranted.
